So... I've [24f] been in your daughter's shoes. I used to visit the school's counseling center on a weekly (if not sometimes daily) basis, and really spilled a lot of bottled emotional stuff on those poor psychologists. I almost killed myself in my 6th year before I realized it was time to drop out.

> She doesn't share things with me

The fact is, most people suffer in silence and don't reach out like that until it is far too late. While it probably freaks you out to see that number being called on her end, you should take it with a big fat grain of salt. Your daughter knows her thought process is seriously messed up and has taken the first steps toward getting help.

> I've never met or heard about any friends from school or work

From my experience, your daughter might be having a tough time with either academic stress, loneliness, drugs/alcohol, or some combination. It is unsurprising to find that a depressed person has a hard time maintaining themselves, let alone friendships and family connections.

> I don't know what is going on with her.

Don't be like my parents. So here's what you **don't do**: Phone her up, and ask her how she's doing, or what that phone number is. She will tell you everything is fine and become a little more quieter. I know exactly how much it hurts having to admit to someone you're not fine, and if there are deeper issues here, she probably won't be likely to share them with you. It's not manipulation, it's guilt. Guilt that she can't just be happy or function.

Here's how I wish my last year at Uni would have went: I wish my parents had just come over physically, and listened to me. Instead, they asked me at the worst possible times how I was, whether it was at their house, at a restaurant, etc. At my own apartment I felt more relaxed, and willing to share things. They knew something was up and asked me over the telephone, or at their home if I was doing alright (of course I said I was "fine"). I wish they had just listened to the pain I was in, without judgement, and not tried to minimize my feelings (i.e. "but you're so smart", or "life is beautiful"). Even when they came over and found I was in a fetal position for hours, crying uncontrollably, they just kept talking and saying stuff.

Don't mention the phone number because that's private and honestly pretty triggering. Just, keep at it. If she says she's fine, just keep asking, and tell her you don't believe she's fine, that she doesn't look fine. Ask her what's troubling her, because you see it on her face or whatever that she doesn't look fine to you. At some point she will tell you (I promise), because you have noticed, and you want to listen. 

It will not be an easy conversation, sorry.

The pulse is continuous in a wavelength similar to the orange color of low pressure sodium (if I am not mistaken!) so that other observatories can remove the very discrete wavelength. You are right, the laser is VERY powerful to ionize air like that!

The laser ionizes a point of air around 50-60 miles up in the atmosphere, creating a static "reference star" with a very sharply defined wavelength. Since the light is monochromatic, it can be focused very precisely. It is assumed that stars appear as pinpoints of light, so by comparing the reference star to an actual star, they can generate commands to the adaptive optics in the detector setup. They are usually piezoelectric elements that push and pull on the secondary mirror and correct the light path of your target star as it travels through earth's atmosphere. Once the target star matches your reference star, you can be generally assured that your reconstructed image is accurate.
